common_name: Akishino Temari Mountain Hydrangea (Double Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to partial sun.

directions: Akishino Temari is a petite mountain hydrangea whose ring of double sterile florets grows so dense it nearly hides the small fertile flowers at the center, giving a mophead-like fullness unusual for this species. Blooms open white in early summer, then shift through pink or blue depending on soil acidity before aging to a muted green with a lingering pink eye, so a single flower head can show several colors at once over its long season. It stays compact and well-suited to small shade gardens, blooming on old wood, so prune only to shape immediately after flowering. Keep soil consistently moist and give it bright shade rather than full sun to preserve flower color and avoid leaf scorch.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Beni-yama Mountain Hydrangea (Red Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, or full sun where soil stays reliably moist.

directions: Beni-yama is an old Japanese mountain hydrangea selection whose flat lacecap heads open white in early summer and quickly flush through pink to a vivid scarlet red, usually keeping paler, near-white centers around a core of lilac-blue fertile flowers. Its pointed, mid-green leaves are flushed crimson both when young in spring and again in autumn, echoing the flower color. It is a vigorous, easy-to-grow, upright shrub that blooms on old wood, so limit pruning to shaping cuts made right after flowering. It tolerates open, sunny sites better than many mountain hydrangeas but still colors and performs best with some afternoon shade.

common_name: Mount Aso Mountain Hydrangea (Pink Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Mount Aso, named for the Japanese volcano where it was first found, is a low, wide-spreading mountain hydrangea with very flat lacecap heads whose outer sterile florets twist into a distinctive propeller shape. Sepals read deep pink to lilac-blue or purple depending on soil pH, each with a contrasting blue eye, surrounding a center of small bluish fertile flowers. Its bushy, medium-growing habit stays low and broad rather than upright, and the foliage turns red, orange, and purple in autumn. It blooms on old wood, so confine pruning to light shaping immediately after the flowers fade.

common_name: Hakucho Mountain Hydrangea (Swan Double White Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; tolerates some drought once established.

directions: Hakucho, whose name means swan, is a small Japanese mountain hydrangea originally found growing wild on Mount Fuji, with narrow, almost willow-like leaves and dainty lacecap flower heads. The doubled, pure white sterile florets ring a small fertile center, giving a star-like, lacy effect that fades to soft pink as the blooms age. It is less vigorous and free-flowering than many mountain hydrangeas and prefers a shaded site, but is fairly drought tolerant once established for a plant of this type. Prune only lightly right after flowering, since buds for the next season form on old wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Omacha Variegata Mountain Hydrangea (O-amacha Nishiki Variegated Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light or open shade with protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Omacha Variegata is a variegated-leaf sport of the mountain hydrangea Oamacha, opening new leaves golden yellow with a thin red margin before they mature to green mottled with gold toward the center, and turning red-burgundy in fall. Its small lacecap flowers open white and age to pink or blue depending on soil acidity, typically appearing a little later in the season than other mountain hydrangea cultivars. It grows into a compact, rounded shrub and tolerates full sun but develops its best leaf color and flowering in cool, lightly shaded conditions with morning sun and afternoon shade. As with other mountain hydrangeas it flowers on old wood, so prune only to shape immediately after bloom.
